text: The Sisters' Islands and Singapore's First Marine Park
Two small wooded islands sit side by side south of Sentosa, so close together that from the sea they look like a pair.
A Malay legend says they were once two sisters who drowned there in a storm.

In the colonial era soldiers fired howitzers at targets on them, in the 1970s they were reclaimed into picnic islands with swimming lagoons, and since 2014 they have been the heart of Singapore's first marine park, where hawksbill turtles now nest and hatch.
The islands are Pulau Subar Laut, Big Sister's Island, which faces the open sea, and Pulau Subar Darat, Small Sister's Island, which faces the mainland.
In Malay, laut means seaward and darat landward.
A narrow but deep channel runs between them, with currents strong enough to make swimming across dangerous.
The best-known version of the legend, as the National Library tells it, is about two sisters, Minah and Linah.
A pirate chief seized Linah and carried her off in his boat.
Minah swam after them and was overcome by a wave, and Linah threw herself overboard to join her sister.
After a storm, two islands appeared where the sisters had drowned, and the villagers named them after the pair.
Other versions differ in the details, but in all of them the sisters end up together as the two islands.
Before the 1970s the islands were smaller than they are today, and in the colonial era they had a military use.
In March 1905 the Straits Times carried a notice that howitzer practice would be held "at the targets on Sisters Island" the following week.
After independence the Southern Islands were turned into places for recreation.
In 1974 and 1975, reclamation added about 5.4 hectares to the two islands, and seawalls were built along the reef edges to enclose sandy swimming lagoons.
A 1975 report in the Straits Times described Belgian contractors helping to reclaim Kusu, the Sisters, Hantu, Sebarok and Coney.
From 1976 the Sentosa Development Corporation looked after the islands, and by the late 1970s community centres and youth groups were running Sunday picnics there.
The reclamation that made the beaches also buried much of the islands' reef flats.
Across Singapore, the reefs suffered far more from decades of land reclamation, dredging of shipping channels and dumping of earth, which clouded the water and smothered corals.
Marine scientists at the National University of Singapore estimate that the country's reef area shrank from about 39.85 square kilometres in 1953 to about 13.25 square kilometres in 2012.
Underwater visibility, which was about 10 metres in the early 1960s, fell to 2 or 3 metres, and corals now grow only in shallower water.
Most of the reefs that survive fringe the Southern Islands, among them the Sisters.
In 2009, a group of marine scientists and nature enthusiasts put forward a Blue Plan for Singapore's seas, which called for protected areas for the remaining reefs.
On the 12th of July 2014, at the Festival of Biodiversity, the Minister of State for National Development, Desmond Lee, announced that Singapore would establish its first marine park.
The Sisters' Islands Marine Park covers about 40 hectares: the two islands and the waters around them, and the western reefs of Saint John's Island and Pulau Tekukor.

Free guided walks on the islands' intertidal shores began in August 2014, a public gallery on Saint John's Island opened in July 2015, and two dive trails, a shallow one and a deeper one, opened in September 2015.
The park has become a base for research and restoration.
In 2011 a Neptune's cup sponge, a giant goblet-shaped sponge thought to have died out after 1908, was found again off Saint John's Island.
In 2018 NParks and JTC began lowering eight artificial reef structures, each about 10 metres tall, into the park's waters, for corals to grow on.
In 2018 NParks opened Singapore's first turtle hatchery on Small Sister's Island.
Eggs from nests at risk, laid too close to the waterline or in busy places, are moved there into buried cages and watched until they hatch.
Hawksbill turtles, which are critically endangered, nest on several of Singapore's shores, including Big Sister's Island.
In the 2026 season, by the middle of August, 25 nests had been recorded across Singapore, and 294 hatchlings had emerged from the hatchery.
In 2021 the islands closed for rebuilding, and Big Sister's Island reopened on the 28th of October 2024.

It now has a floating boardwalk that rises and falls with the tide, with coral panels and moon pools, a lagoon turned into a tidal pool, a coastal forest trail and a view deck on the island's highest point.
Solar panels power a small desalination plant.
Small Sister's Island stays closed to the public as a zone for conservation and research.
Visitors reach Big Sister's Island by ferry from Marina South Pier, a trip of about half an hour that stops at Saint John's Island.
Where it fits in the bigger story: The Sisters' Islands have been remade several times, from a legend to an artillery target, a reclaimed picnic spot and now a marine park.

Their story mirrors that of Singapore's reefs as a whole, which lost most of their area to the growth of the city and the port, and the park is one of the ways the country is trying to keep what remains.
